result.markdown: --- title: "[Graph.intersection()]{.doc-object-name .doc-function .doc-label .doc-label-method}" body-classes: doc-api-page doc-py-api-page shift-heading-level-by: 0 toc-depth: 3 page-navigation: false html-table-processing: none --- ::: {.doc-subject} Compute the intersection of this graph with another graph. ::: ::: {.doc-usage-source} Usage [Source](https://github.com/rich-iannone/edgecase/blob/main/python/edgecase/graph.py#L15636-L15707){target="_blank" rel="noopener"} ::: ::: {.doc-signature .doc-Kind.FUNCTION} ```python Graph.intersection(other) ``` ::: ::: {.doc-text} ![Intersection](/assets/graphs/intersection.light.svg){.lightbox fig-alt="G and H share edges A–B and B–D; A–C is only in G (accent) and C–D only in H (teal). The intersection keeps just the shared edges A–B and B–D; A–C and C–D are dashed, and node C, left with no edges, is dropped too." width="100%"} Returns a new graph containing only edges that exist in both graphs. Nodes are included only if they are endpoints of common edges. ::: ## Parameters {.doc-parameters} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [other]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [Graph]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : The graph to intersect with. ::: ## Returns {.doc-returns} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [Graph]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : A new graph containing edges present in both graphs. ::: ## Raises {.doc-raises} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [ValueError]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : If the graphs have different directedness. ::: ## Technical Notes {.doc-technical-notes} Intersection keeps only edges present in both graphs and drops any node that would end up isolated as a result, matching the algebraic identity $E(G_1 \cap G_2) = E_1 \cap E_2$ followed by node pruning. Both operands must share the same directedness. Where both graphs carry a weight, label, or attribute for the same edge or node, the calling graph's value wins and the other graph fills in only what the calling graph lacks, which is worth knowing when weights differ. A common use is identifying the stable core of a network observed at multiple time points. ## Examples {.doc-examples} Only the edges present in both graphs survive -- here, both graphs share edges `1-2` and `2-3`, but the triangle's closing edge and the square's extra edges don't overlap: ::: {#4100a2d6 .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.python .cell-code} import edgecase as ec # Triangle g1 = ec.Graph(directed=False) for i in range(1, 4): g1.add_node() g1.add_edge(1, 2) g1.add_edge(2, 3) g1.add_edge(3, 1) # Square with diagonal g2 = ec.Graph(directed=False) for i in range(1, 5): g2.add_node() g2.add_edge(1, 2) g2.add_edge(2, 3) g2.add_edge(3, 4) g2.add_edge(4, 1) common = g1.intersection(g2) common.count_edges() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ``` 2 ``` ::: ::: This is useful for finding stable connections that exist at multiple time points or in multiple network versions.
